sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct 1 proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding. 1. Introduction Video generation has advanced rapidly in realism, but precise control over how scene unfolds remains challenging [6, 21, 31]. Generated videos may contain incorrect interactions, inconsistent spatial relationships, or discontinuities across shots, even when individual frames appear plausible [2, 23]. Text prompts and reference images provide semantic and appearance guidance, but often leave object trajectories, camera behavior, and event timing implicit [12, 28]. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, complement these inputs by representing scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order in coarse video sequence. While structural proxies offer more explicit control over scene organization, their guidance is not without limitations, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In the bakery scene, text-only generation introduces an abrupt spatial shift and changes object details across shots, while proxy guidance helps preserve scene layout and object continuity. Similar improvements are observed in the dynamic-action and multi-view examples. However, proxy guidance often contains low-fidelity geometry and motion that may mislead the generator and hinder realistic scene realization, as illustrated by the low-poly donuts in the bakery example. What should be preserved from the proxy and what should be refined ultimately depends on the users intent, making additional conditions, such as text and reference images, essential for guiding the generation. This raises central question: how can generators preserve useful proxy constraints without inheriting their artifacts or overlooking information from other conditions? Existing benchmarks provide limited insight into how these requirements interact in proxy-guided generation. To address this gap, we identify three complementary abilities essential for successful proxy-guided generation: Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind additional conditions to the appropriate entities and events. To evaluate these abilities, we introduce ProxyGenBench, comprising 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across dynamic action, multi-shot storytelling, and multi-view consistency challenges. Our scenes cover four potential applications of proxyguided generation: enhancing reference-to-video workflows, enabling code-driven proxy authoring, supporting game-like world modeling, and assisting 3D animation completion. For each scene, we provide multiple variants to study how models respond to different levels of conditioning detail and balance guidance across modalities. Low-fidelity proxies leave more room for refinement but may provide insufficient structural guidance, while high-fidelity proxies are easier to follow but risk transferring unwanted details. Similarly, simple text prompts may underspecify user intent, whereas detailed prompts or additional image references may distract models from the proxy. Through matched and targeted configurations, we examine when proxies improve control, how proxy fidelity affects completion, and whether additional conditions are correctly integrated into the generated scene. To evaluate model performance across these variations, we organize 32 fine-grained criteria into eight capabilities under Preserve, Complete, and Bind, and instantiate applicable criteria as verified, case-specific checklist questions. Each checklist is grounded in the inputs available to the generator and fixed across models for the same case. VLM judgments use visual or audio evidence to assess structural adherence, completion, and binding beyond proxy resemblance. We report the three dimension scores alongside structure-sensitive Strict score, which gives additional emphasis to critical Preserve constraints because structural control is the basic requirement of proxy-guided generation. Experiments on five video generators show that proxy guidance improves spatiotemporal control, particularly action transitions and cross-shot spatial consistency. However, high average Preserve score does not guarantee that all critical structural constraints are satisfied together. In scene-matched comparisons, moving from coarse to detailed proxies increases Preserve but lowers Complete for all five models, revealing preservationcompletion tension. Results on Studio 3D proxies also show that strong structural adherence can coexist with incorrect condition binding. Together, these findings highlight the need to preserve intended structure selectively, correct proxy artifacts, and ground supplementary information within the same generated scene. Our contributions are threefold: Benchmark. We build controlled proxy-guided generation cases varying proxy detail and text, image, and audio requirements. Evaluation. We develop verified, case-specific checklists to assess intended structural constraints, completion of unfinished content, correction of proxy artifacts, and grounding of additional conditions. Analysis. We quantify proxy benefits and characterize joint structural, completion, and condition-binding challenges across input variations. 2 2. Related Work 2.1. Controllable Video Generation Video generation has increasingly adopted spatial and temporal conditions to complement text and reference images. VideoComposer [27] combines multiple control signals, Motion Prompting [10] uses trajectories to guide scene motion, and SymphoMotion [32] jointly controls camera and object motion. VideoDirectorGPT [18] uses LLM-guided planning to maintain layout and entity consistency across multiple scenes. 3D Scene Prompting [17] uses scene geometry to maintain consistency across viewpoints. More directly related, Proxy2World [29] explores synthesizing detailed videos from lightweight structural proxies and the balance between structural adherence and visual quality. These methods demonstrate the value of spatiotemporal guidance. Our ProxyGenBench instead studies structural inputs that leave content unspecified or contain artifacts requiring correction. 2.2. Video Generation Benchmarks Existing benchmarks assess complementary aspects of generated videos. VBench [14] and EvalCrafter [19] evaluate visual quality, temporal consistency, and semantic alignment; VBench-2.0 [33] and VideoPhy [5] extend evaluation toward physical realism and commonsense. VideoScore [13] and EvalVerse [30] further assess human-aligned and cinematic quality. T2V-CompBench [24] examines compositional requirements such as attribute binding and object interactions, while TC-Bench [9] focuses on temporal state and relation changes. Concurrent work PROWBench [15] evaluates fidelity to program-specified world states and events, including proxy-conditioned generation. ProxyGenBench instead focuses on imperfect structural proxies, requiring models to preserve intended spatial and temporal relationships, correct proxy artifacts, and bind supplementary conditions within the same scene. Varying proxy detail and complementary inputs lets us examine how these requirements interact. 3. ProxyGenBench ProxyGenBench evaluates how different input conditions affect video generation. It tests whether models can preserve the intended scene structure, complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and integrate additional text, image, and audio conditions. These challenges often arise together, but model may perform well on some while struggling with others. 3.1. Problem Setting and Structural Proxies Structural proxy. structural proxy is video that specifies the intended scene layout, object placement, motion, camera behavior, and event order without fully defining the final result. Our proxies are rendered from 3D representations obtained from various sources. They may contain Figure 2. Evaluation case construction. We use proxy fidelity to describe the level of geometric and motion detail, rather than content accuracy. higher-fidelity proxy is thus not necessarily more accurate. Generation setting. We define each evaluation case as = (s, p, ), where is the intended scene specification, is structural proxy, and includes text prompt and optional image or audio references. Given (p, ), the model generates video v. The scene specification is used only for benchmark evaluation and is not provided to the video model. We derive evaluation checklists only from the conditions available to the model, ensuring that it is not evaluated on information it never received. Details are in the appendix. 3.2. Benchmark Construction We construct the benchmark by varying several aspects of proxy-guided video generation. Scene tasks define the spatial and temporal relationships to preserve. Proxy sources and fidelity levels determine how much scene structure is provided and what remains incomplete. Additional text, image, and audio inputs introduce further requirements for the same scene. These variations test different aspects of the same generation problem rather than separate tasks. Scene tasks. Dynamic action tests motion, interactions, and state transitions; multi-shot storytelling tests event order and continuity across cuts; and multi-view consistency tests stable scene and object states across viewpoints. These tasks cover motion, cross-shot continuity, and cross-view consistency; each task is also evaluated on the completion and reference-grounding requirements that apply to it. We additionally annotate five content categoriesCharacters, Navigation, Objects, Combat & Transform, and Camerato describe coverage rather than create separate tasks. Proxy sources. We collect proxies from four source groups, each with different construction workflow  (Fig. 3)  . Enhanced R2V adds proxy guidance to existing imageor audio-conditioned tasks. Native Code-to-Proxy uses an 3 Figure 3. Proxy sources and benchmark coverage: 60 scenes and 312 cases from four source groups. Game Proxy includes game footage and 3D game assets. Source-group and content-category counts are scene-level; input-condition counts are case-level and non-exclusive. LLM-based agent to animate 3D scenes from scripts or reference videos. Game Proxy includes game footage and 3D game assets, while Studio 3D Proxy uses unfinished production assets. Together, these sources cover range of incomplete geometry and motion, with different types of artifacts across sources. We provide details of each construction workflow and its associated proxy artifacts in the appendix. Input variations. We create multiple evaluation cases from each scene by varying the input conditions. We define three proxy-fidelity levelsPr0 (Blockout), Pr1 (Figure), and Pr2 (Detail)with increasing geometric and motion detail. Comparing these levels allows us to study whether more proxy detail improves both structural adherence and natural completion. Text-detail levels T0T2 vary the amount of semantic guidance. Optional image and audio references add requirements for appearance, voice, and events. We vary text detail at fixed proxy level (Pr0) and proxy fidelity at fixed text level (T2)  (Fig. 2)  . This allows us to study their effects separately without testing every combination. Evaluation cases. We construct 312 cases from 60 scenes  (Fig. 2)  , including 294 proxy-conditioned cases and 18 noproxy counterparts. The proxytext grid contains 257 cases, including 60 reference cases. We add 15 no-image, 8 noaudio, and 18 no-proxy cases, plus 14 targeted cases that vary joint reference removal, identity, voice, event timing, or camera control. We separately analyze the Studio 3D proxy subset across five models, while the targeted input variations are examined individually in the appendix. The configurations allow us to compare the effects of proxy availability, input detail, and reference grounding. Full case assignments and evaluation protocols are provided in the appendix. 3.3. Evaluation Framework proxy specifies only part of the intended video, so matching the proxy alone does not guarantee successful generation. Instead, we use case-specific checklists to assess whether the generated video retains the intended structure, completes or corrects unfinished content, and binds supplementary conditions to the correct entities and events (Table 1 and Fig. 4). Evaluation dimensions. Preserve (P1P3) tracks whether intended scene structure, motion, camera behavior, and event continuity survive generation. Complete (C1C3) assesses whether the incomplete proxy is realized as coherent appearance, natural articulation, and plausible interactions instead of carrying over abstraction artifacts. Bind (B1B2) assesses whether text, image, and audio conditions are correctly associated with entities, actions, and moments within that same structure. In the bakery example  (Fig. 4)  , the model must preserve the seating arrangement and event order, turn rigid proxy gestures into natural interactions, and bind the specified clothing and voice references to the correct characters. On matched subsets, action-transition accuracy rises from 0.894 to 1.000, cross-shot spatial consistency from 0.833 to 0.952, and MEt3R [3] error falls from 0.464 to 0.337. These comparisons establish benefits for the measured structural controls, while motion quality and condition binding require separate evaluation. 4.3. Joint Structural Success Average Preserve scores do not show whether all critical structural checks hold in the same output  (Table 3)  . Without independent audio references, Seedance-2.5 and Kling4.0 lead Strict (0.450 and 0.425), yet their Joint Success rates are only 14.0% and 15.0%. Thus, stronger overall performance does not eliminate the preservationcompletion tension, but models differ in how they balance these requirements.

Conclusion ProxyGenBench evaluates three interacting requirements of video generation from imperfect structural proxies: Preserve, Complete, and Bind. Across five models, proxy guidance improves spatiotemporal control, yet strong average adherence can mask violations of joint structural constraints. More detailed proxies can also reduce completion scores, while preserved structure does not ensure correct condition binding. These findings highlight the need for selective control: generators must retain intended structural constraints while correcting proxy artifacts and grounding supplementary information in the same scene.

sections.content: A. Benchmark Construction A.1. Proxy and Text Fidelity Proxy levels. For each scene, we define up to three proxy levels, r0, r1, and r2. When multiple levels are available, they preserve the same story, shot structure, camera plan, blocking, role colours, and key trajectories, while varying primarily in geometric detail and motion fidelity. For Blender-authored proxies, r0 uses coarse coloured primitives; r1 adds articulated bodies and readable props; and r2 remains untextured but provides clearer geometry and more faithful motion. For proxies from other sources, the available levels may have source-specific representations and may not span all three levels; nevertheless, they follow the same abstract-to-detailed ordering, with r0 denoting the most abstract representation, as shown in Fig. 6. Text prompt levels. We define three text-prompt levels, T0, T1, and T2, which progressively increase the amount of semantic and temporal information supplied beyond the proxy video (Figure 7). T0 provides concise target description including the intended visual domain, principal subjects, setting, and key transformationwhile relying primarily on the proxy for shot order, camera framing, blocking, and motion. T1 additionally specifies the desired appearance of characters, objects, and environment, together with coarse shot-level actions and temporal beats. T2 gives the most complete specification: detailed visual attributes, physical and interaction constraints, cinematographic instructions, negative constraints, audio requirements when applicable, and time-resolved plan aligned with the proxy. Across all levels, the proxy remains the primary structural signal; the prompt directs the model to recreate the intended scene with the desired appearance and realism. Controlled case construction. Each scene is organized as controlled experiment with shared target story, duration, generation settings, and reference conditions. The possible core configurations (when the corresponding proxy levels are available) are or instruction. Four cases test voice assignment in two dialogue scenes: in the normal version, each character uses their designated voice reference; in the swapped version, the two characters exchange voice references. The remaining cases test whether models follow specific identity reference, assign the correct image to the correct role, delay the closing of gate, distinguish camera movement from zoom, shift focus at the intended time, keep centered camera while moving through doorway, or operate without both image and audio references. These controls test whether model uses each condition for its intended purpose rather than relying on an easier but incorrect cue. A.2. Proxy Construction Source workflows. Proxies originate from four source groups. Enhanced R2V adds animated structural guidance to reference-to-video tasks; Native Code-to-Proxy animates three-dimensional scenes from scripts or optional reference clips through an LLM-based authoring process; Game Proxy uses game footage or native game assets and animation; and Studio 3D Proxy uses unfinished production scenes. These groups provide heterogeneous incompleteness and artifact patterns, rather than interchangeable samples of one authoring pipeline. The four workflows span reference-conditioned content, script-authored scenes, game environments, and unfinished animation assets, providing distinct sources of missing detail and imperfect motion. Blender-authored proxies and native hierarchies. In the Blender-authored examples, lower-detail proxies contain color-coded primitives, while more detailed versions replace these with articulated figures, distinguishable props, and more informative local motion. Native 3D hierarchies and unfinished studio assets retain source-specific geometric representations and animation. When multiple levels are present, the target story and major camera and event structure are kept consistent; not every source provides every fidelity level. The level labels describe the amount of structural and motion detail, not the correctness of all depicted details. A.3. Scene Coverage {P r0-T0, r0-T1, r0-T2, r1-T2, r2-T2}. The r0-T0,1,2 cases vary text specificity at fixed proxy fidelity, while r0,1,2-T2 varies proxy detail and motion fidelity at fixed detailed text. In addition to the proxytext grid and the input ablations described below, we include 14 targeted control cases. Each keeps the same scene goal but changes one specific input Scene tasks identify the principal structural challenge: dynamic action, multi-shot storytelling, or multi-view consistency. Separately, five content-category annotations describe scene subject matter: Characters (22), Navigation (17), Objects (11), Combat & Transform (7), and Camera (3). The proxy-source, task, and content-category annotations serve distinct roles and should not be interpreted as three mutually exclusive partitions of the same type. 11 Figure 6. Image and independent audio references appear in 177 and 60 cases, respectively; reference-type counts are non-exclusive. Target Conditions Text prompts communicate intended appearance, interactions, sound, and target style in addition to any structural requirements conveyed by the proxy. Reference images can specify identity, clothing, objects, and appearance, while independent audio references can specify voice/source identity or sound events. Such requirements are evaluated for the entity or event to which they are assigned, not merely for their appearance somewhere in the video. Intended stylization versus artifacts. Proxy fidelity is not style target by default. Intended stylization, including intentionally simplified geometry or stylized movement, is described in the accompanying text and is not counted as an unintended proxy artifact. By contrast, proxy placeholders, rigid pseudo-actions, clipping, or missing articulation are completion or correction targets only when the generators supplied conditions support that expectation. checklist must not introduce stylistic requirements from the hidden scene specification alone. This distinction is established before viewing model outputs. Audio references. Agent-Assisted Construction and Verification Our construction process combines LLM-assisted authoring with iterative inspection and correction, as illustrated in Fig. 8. An agent converts shared scene specification into executable Blender scenes and English prompts. We then inspect the rendered proxies, source files, and packaged inputs, correcting inconsistencies before finalizing the benchmark cases. The figure illustrates the general workflow, although the inspection process and available evidence vary across scenes. Native 3D and Studio 3D sources use separate construction pipelines. Shared scene specification. Construction begins with story brief and the behavior to be tested, such as object persistence, role correspondence, or camera-motion control. The agent expands the brief into timed storyboard specifying shot order, camera framing and movement, character blocking, key trajectories, and relevant object-state changes. This storyboard guides both proxy construction and prompt authoring (Fig. 8, steps 12). Stable role colours identify characters and salient objects within the proxies, while text and appearance references specify their intended final appearance. Proxy-level construction. For Blender-authored scenes, the agent receives explicit instructions for each available fidelity level (Fig. 8, step 3a). At r0, characters use coarse body blocks and root motion, with minimal arms or contact markers when essential to communicate an interaction. At r1, articulated heads, torsos, and limbs provide clearer poses and object interactions. At r2, additional geometry improves hands, feet, prop silhouettes, and local scene readability, together with fuller motion. Materials remain simple and untextured across these levels. The execution harness runs the agents generated bpy code in Blender and returns execution output, errors, scene information, and requested preview renders. The agent uses this feedback to construct and repair the scene incrementally before the final animation render. Where geometry-swap mode is used, new tier starts from an existing animated proxy: replacement geometry inherits the original objects animation through shared parent, while instructions preserve cameras, frame range, frame rate, timeline structure, role colours, and existing trajectories. These constraints guide the intended differences between levels; rendered inspection remains necessary to detect unintended changes. Native game and studio assets retain their available source representations and do not necessarily follow this Blenderauthoring procedure. Text-level construction and reference binding. The agent generates three levels of English prompts from the 14 shared storyboard (Fig. 8, step 3b). Each proxy-conditioned prompt begins with instructions on how to use the reference video, followed by description of the intended final video. T0 provides broad semantic and visual goal, relying mainly on the proxy for spatial and temporal structure. T1 adds appearance details and coarse descriptions of actions and shots. T2 provides detailed requirements for appearance, interactions, camera work, timing, and sound when applicable. We review the prompt content to maintain these distinctions and shorten overly detailed T0 prompts when necessary. The proxy guides scene layout, camera motion, timing, and object movement, while text and appearance references specify characters, materials, environments, and visual style. Image and audio references are numbered according to their order in the input arrays. Input ablations retain the same target scene and remaining references, with prompts specifying the conditions available in each case. Appearance and voice requirements are expressed in text where needed in the absence of the corresponding reference media. We use increasing character budgets as authoring guidelines: approximately 1,0002,000 for T0, 2,5003,500 for T1, and 4,0005,000 for T2, including proxy and reference instructions. Prompt lengths reflect scene complexity and the information required at each level. The same finalized case prompt is used across supported models. Optional voice-reference conversion. For some existing R2V cases with Chinese voice references, we automatically transcribe and translate the recordings into English, then synthesize English speech using voices cloned from the original recordings (Fig. 8, step 3c). These translated recordings serve as voice references, not as dialogue that the generated video must reproduce. The conversion targets speaker identity, intended meaning, and approximate speaking duration rather than exact word-level timing. Processed recordings are assigned to the corresponding numbered audio conditions and serve as references for generation and evaluation. We retain original recordings and conversion metadata where available and leave mixed-speaker or speech-with-music recordings unchanged. Timeline verification with Blender sources. For audited scenes with available Blender files, we check explicit prompt timelines against both the source scene and the rendered proxy (Fig. 8, step 4). Source inspection includes frame range and frame rate, camera assignments, timeline markers, relevant animation keyframes, and, where needed, sampled camera transforms and focal lengths. These provide supporting evidence for intended event timing, shot boundaries, and camera behavior. Frame indices are converted to seconds using the scenes starting frame and frame rate. We cross-check source evidence with sampled video frames, including adjacent frames around proposed cuts and frames surrounding important actions or state changes. timeline marker may describe an action rather than cut, and camera assignment need not produce visible cut when successive views coincide. We therefore distinguish source annotations from events visible in the rendered video. When the evidence supports continuous shot, the prompt describes successive action beats without introducing additional cuts. These checks establish structure only to the extent supported by the proxy. Coarse geometry may show trajectory or an objects broad location without establishing finger contact, subtle facial acting, or physical plausibility. Silent proxies cannot verify speech, knocks, or breathing. Such details remain target-generation instructions rather than claims about evidence present in the proxy. Targeted correction and packaging. Corrections address specific observed defects and are followed by re-inspection (Fig. 8, step 5). For example, in The key under the cup, hand in the intermediate proxy appeared too close to the cup during the reaction shot. targeted repair instruction moved both hands away while preserving camera cuts, framing, role colours, and the cup and key trajectories. Later source and rendered-frame checks supported the cuts at 4 and 8 seconds. When the proxy agrees with the intended scene but an explicit prompt description conflicts with it, we revise the prompt to match the proxy. We organize the corrected inputs into benchmark cases (Fig. 8, step 6). In the P/C/B evaluation pipeline, Qwen3.5-397BA17B screens the checklist questions before video scoring. Criterion boundaries. The categorization is determined by the requirement being tested, not solely by the visual phenomenon. Preserve measures proxy-specified structure; Complete measures realization of unspecified content and correction of unintended proxy abstraction; Bind measures assignment of text, image, and audio conditions to the designated entities and events. For example, P1.1 checks the 17 number of entities, whereas C1.1 checks their realized appearance. Similarly, P2 checks whether coarse proxy trajectory is respected, C2 judges the naturalness of the motion, and B2 checks whether an action is assigned to the specified actor. Matched Fidelity Trends We analyze the effect of proxy fidelity on 31 matched scenes, with all three proxy levels (P r0, r1, and r2), fixed T2 text, and no independent audio references. Table 13 reports the model-level changes from r0 to r2. All five models exhibit higher mean Preserve and lower mean Complete at r2 than at r0, while Bind responds differently across models. Notably, Seedance-2.5 gains 0.040 in Bind, whereas MiniMax-H3 loses 0.182, indicating that stronger proxy guidance does not necessarily facilitate reference grounding. The intermediate fidelity level reveals further distinction. Averaged equally across models, Preserve increases from 0.738 at r0 to 0.776 at r1, but slightly decreases to 0.767 at r2. In contrast, Complete declines monotonically from 0.601 to 0.554 and 0.538. Most of the completion loss therefore occurs between r0 and r1 (-0.047), with smaller additional decline from r1 to r2 (-0.016). The corresponding average scores = (0.696, 0.668, 0.665) show that additional proxy detail does not translate into higher overall performance. These results suggest diminishing structural benefits alongside persistent completion costs, rather than uniformly beneficial increase in proxy fidelity. C.2. Scene-Level Variation To examine whether the fidelity trade-off holds across individual scenes, we analyze 155 matched modelscene pairs from the same 31 scenes. Table 14 and Fig. 9 summarize the joint changes in Preserve and Complete from r0 to r2. Notably, 49 of 155 pairs (31.6%) exhibit reduced Complete without improved Preserve, indicating that additional proxy detail can incur completion costs without corresponding structural benefits. Conversely, 29 pairs (18.7%) improve Preserve without sacrificing Complete. Scene-cluster bootstrap estimates further show that the Complete decline (C = 0.063, 95% CI [0.082, 0.043]) is more consistent than the Preserve improvement (P = +0.029, 95% CI [0.030, +0.095]). These results highlight the importance of selectively exploiting proxy guidance rather than uniformly following additional proxy detail. Figure 9. Scene-level Preserve and Complete changes from r0 to r2 (155 matched observations). C.3. Completion Bottleneck visual or motion quality. To identify which capabilities drive the preservation completion tension, we further decompose the fidelity results into eight capabilities. Using the same 31 matched T2 scenes and five models, Table 15 reports the model-averaged changes from r0 to r2, together with scene-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and the direction of change across scenes. The completion decline is dominated by C3 (Proxy Abstraction Handling), which decreases by 0.104 (95% CI: [-0.151, -0.057]) and shows negative changes in 24 of 31 scenes. Its decline is more than twice that of C2 (-0.048) and accounts for approximately 55% of the summed decreases across the three Complete capabilities. C1 also exhibits smaller but consistent decline (-0.036), whereas the uncertainty interval for C2 overlaps zero. In contrast, all three Preserve capabilities show positive mean changes but substantial scene-level variability, with confidence intervals spanning zero. This reveals an asymmetry in how models respond to increased proxy detail: structural adherence may improve, but the ability to replace proxy abstractions with completed appearance and motion becomes more challenging. The particularly large decline in C3 suggests that the main difficulty lies in distinguishing useful structural guidance from proxy-specific details that should be refined, rather than uniform deterioration in D. Limitations and Future Work Limitations. Our proxy fidelity levels jointly vary geometric and motion detail, making it difficult to isolate their individual effects. Moreover, evaluating subtle physical interactions and precise audiovisual synchronization remains challenging for current VLM-based evaluators. Future Work. Our findings motivate more effective proxyguided generation methods that selectively preserve intended structure while refining incomplete geometry and motion. Future research could explore adaptive proxy conditioning and proxy-aware training to better balance Preserve and Complete, alongside stronger entityand event-level multimodal grounding to improve Bind. To further identify challenging evaluation capabilities, we examine 611 judge-labeled failures at the capability level  (Table 21)  .
